newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says 400,000 E Europe coal workers face sack.
newsitem.headline: UN says 400,000 E Europe coal workers face sack.

text.p: Coal industry privatisation in eastern Europe has caused half a million job losses since the start of painful market reforms and another 400,000 workers face the sack in coming years, a U.N. forecast said on Wednesday.

The U.N. Economic Commission for Europe (ECE), quoting industry data from eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, said Poland suffered the biggest job cuts between 1990 and 1996 with 150,000 workers sacked, followed by Russia with 147,000.

In the same period, Romania shut down 12 coal mines at a cost of 60,000 jobs. An equal number of jobs were lost in the Czech Republic with 15 mines closed, 20,000 in Hungary and 20 mines, 2,000 in Bulgaria and another 2,000 in Slovenia.
"By the year 2000, it is expected that 376,000 to 400,000 additional jobs will have been cut in central and eastern Europe," said the forecast, based on industry estimates.
It said governments would continue to intervene to sustain output in eastern European countries undergoing restructuring.
An ECE survey in October forecast total hard coal output in eastern and western Europe at 534 million tonnes in 1996.

This figure does not include output in Kazahkstan, the second biggest producer among Soviet successor states. Including Kazakhstan, European coal output is forecast to rise to 625.69 million tonnes this year, against 615.31 million in 1995.

In 1995, European hard coal output was 535 million tonnes, after falling by about 30 million from 1994, the ECE said. Production represented 19 per cent of global output last year against 25 per cent in 1990.
The decline in European coal production, mainly mined underground and under difficult geological conditions, has accelerated since 1990.
